newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Aluminium powers to highest since late 1995.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Aluminium powers to highest since late 1995.

text.p: Industrial metals grabbed the commodity market limelight on Friday as investors pounced on the London Metal Exchange's (LME) aluminium contract as the next candidate for a supply squeeze.
Also in the metals complex, tin climbed another $100 a tonne and nickel headed higher after workers at a Canadian producer went on strike.

The appearance of nearby delivery premiums in the aluminium market drew speculative money into the benchmark three months delivery futures, sending it upto $1,740 a tonne, up $39 from Thursday and the highest level seen since November 1995.
"They think that if a squeeze develops in August and September dates it will lift the whole market structure," a trader said.
The potential squeeze is believed to involve a call options granter with a large uncovered position in August and September.
Aluminium market fundamentals were also tending to favour the bulls with analysts generally forecasting western world supply deficits until the end of the century.

Researchers at brokers GNI reckoned that as long as the one million tonnes of idled production capacity at western aluminium smelters was not restarted in one go, the market will be in a supply deficit through 1998, with the possibility of a capacity squeeze in 1999.
It said aluminium prices were a long term bargain, forecasting $2,500 a tonne within the next two years.
Tin prices continued their strong bounce which has been fuelled by speculative buying, shortcovering and good demand on the Malaysian physical market.
Friday's peak of $5,655 a tonne was $325 above the week's low but some chartists see it running into strong resistance on any further move towards $5,700.

A not unexpected strike by workers at a nickel mine and smelter at Sudbury, Ontario, owned by Canada's Falconbridge, produced a relatively small $50 rise in the three months price on the LME, to $7,485 a tonne.

It produced 45,700 tonnes of nickel, 50,000 tonnes of copper and 1,600 tonnes of cobalt in 1996 but traders reckon the strike will have to continue for more than just a few days before it begins to affect the supply pipeline.
